newsitem.title: UK: Wheat prices seen see-sawing despite bumper crops.
newsitem.headline: Wheat prices seen see-sawing despite bumper crops.

text.p: Wheat prices are likely to fluctuate in the coming months as world markets continue to operate on tight stocks despite bumper harvests, a leading monitor of grains said on Thursday.

Favourable weather and good yields across the world sent benchmark Chicago wheat futures to below $4.00 a bushel for the first time since mid-1995 this week, prompting rival exporters to revive old disputes on government subsidies.
The International Grain Council (IGC), which groups importers and exporters, said the course of prices in the coming months depended on what farmers decide to plant for 1997.
"They have shown us that they can respond to high prices by increasing sowings," said one IGC official, commenting on the Council's latest monthly report on demand and supply.
But they may not be flexible this time -- often, even when prices are declining, there could be a tendency to grow even more, albeit at a lower return per unit, the IGC said.

It was only a few months ago when importers were scrambling to find just any type of reasonably-priced grain while stocks were running at a fragile 20-year low and the weather seemed adverse everywhere.
Now, some producers like Argentina have found themselves so oversupplied that they can sell wheat to traditionally European markets at prices that barely offset the higher Atlantic freight costs .
"Argentina will set the world price," said one IGC official. "It has to sell because it has no storing facilities."

In its report, the IGC increased its 1996 wheat output estimate to 573 million tonnes from a previous 571 million, saying yields were higher than expected in the European Union (EU), China and Australia.
It raised the estimate for the EU to 98.1 million tonnes, compared with last year's 96.1 million while Australia was seen harvesting 20.2 million, up from 17 million due to favouable weather.
Wheat stocks at end of July 1997 were projected unchanged at 104 million tonnes, and while this was 11 million tonnes more than last season, it was still the second lowest since 1980.
"Stocks are rebuilding but it's nothing spectacular," said Bill De Maria, assistant executive director of the IGC.
Coarse grains stocks were estimated five million tonnes higher than last month's forecast at 105 million tonnes, up 21 million from the 1995/96 level.
The IGC attributed the rise to a higher maize crop in the United States this year.
"Harvest weather has been good in most areas with the exception of the southeast, where heavy rains interrupted fieldwork," the IGC said.
Canada was another winner mainly as a result of an increase in acreage.
